## Two Types of Architects

Fowler contrasts two styles of architects: Architectus Reloadus, the "traditional" architect who makes all critical decisions, ensuring the system's conceptual integrity. This approach risks making the architect a bottleneck and undermines team collaboration.

Architectus Oryzus is a collaborative architect who mentors the team, anticipates issues, and fosters technical growth. Instead of making all decisions, this architect empowers the team to handle complex challenges.

## Key Insights

One of the most profound insights from Fowler's essay is that an architect's value is inversely proportional to the number of decisions they make. Additionally, complex systems become hard to change not because of inherent limitations but because of choices made during development, and by designing for flexibility, architects can make systems more resilient to change.

Fowler suggests "guide," as in mountaineering, as a better name—a more experienced and skillful team member who teaches other team members to better fend for themselves yet is always there for the really tricky stuff.

Based on the search results, here's what Gregor Hohpe discusses regarding architect roles in his "Architect Elevator" concept:

## The Architect Elevator Concept

Hohpe pictures the levels of an organization as floors in a building, with architects riding an "architect elevator" to move between a large enterprise's board room and the engine room where software is being built.

## Key Architect Role

The primary role of an architect is to ride the elevators between the penthouse and engine room, stopping wherever needed to support digital efforts: automating software manufacturing, minimizing up-front decision making, and influencing the organization alongside technology evolution.

## Enterprise Architect vs. Other IT Architects

Hohpe makes an important distinction between different architect types. He notes that some IT architects, who aren't enterprise architects, work at enterprise scope—these are technical folks who have learned to ride the elevator to the upper floors to engage with management and business architecture, making them critical elements in any IT transformation.

## Modern Architect's Role

Rather than focus on technical decisions alone, architects and senior technologists need to combine organizational and technical knowledge to effect change in their company's structure and processes, connecting the IT engine room to the penthouse where business strategy is defined.

The "Architect Elevator" metaphor essentially emphasizes architects as bridges between business strategy (penthouse) and technical implementation (engine room), regardless of their specific title.

## Architect Specializations in BTABoK

IASA comprises Business Architects, Information Architects, Software Architects, Infrastructure Architects, and Solution Architects. The BTABoK was written with business, enterprise, solutions, software, information and infrastructure architects and their derivations in mind.

## Key Roles

**Enterprise Architect:** The Enterprise Architect has mastered the fundamental skills in architecture and has been a practicing professional architect within one of the specializations prior to moving into the enterprise architecture practice. The enterprise architect has learned enough of the specializations to lead the architecture teams within an organization and will have functioned as a solutions architect to the extent necessary to lead at the enterprise or global level.

**Solution Architect & Enterprise Architect:** The BTABoK treats both of these as focus areas on generalization, meaning the solution or enterprise architect has a more rounded set of competencies from all 4 depth specializations, and can be seen as generalists who focus on either solution delivery or enterprise scoped technology strategy delivery.

The BTABoK framework is designed to be inclusive of all these specializations and career levels within the architect profession.

A Google Certified Professional - Cloud Architect designs, develops, and manages solutions on Google Cloud. More specifically, a Cloud Architect designs, builds, and manages robust, secure, and scalable cloud solutions to solve business challenges.

The role focuses on designing and planning a cloud solution architecture to managing and provisioning the solution infrastructure. The Cloud Architect should be proficient in all aspects of enterprise cloud strategy, solution design, and architectural best practices.

Additionally, they should be experienced in software development methodologies and approaches including multi-tiered distributed applications that span hybrid or multi-cloud environments.

## Architecture Decision Records (ADRs)

An Architecture Decision Record (ADR) is a short document (typically one to two pages) capturing a single, architecturally significant decision: the context that forced it, the decision itself with full justification, and its consequences. ADRs provide a persistent, queryable history of why a system is built the way it is.

## Technology Radar

A Technology Radar is a tool that documents techniques and technologies, with options to adopt, trial, assess, or hold them. The concept of ADRs was popularised by Michael Nygard and adopted by ThoughtWorks (marked "Adopt" on their Technology Radar).

## Architecture Review Board (ARB) vs. Decentralized Approach

There's an important tension in how organizations approach architectural governance. The State of DevOps report reveals that the traditional approach of Architecture Review Boards is counterproductive, often hindering workflow and correlating with low organizational performance. 

As an alternative, an architectural advice process is a decentralized approach where anyone can make any architectural decision, provided they seek advice from those affected and those with relevant expertise. Practices such as Architecture Decision Records and advisory forums ensure that decisions remain informed, while empowering those closest to the work to make decisions.

## Technology Selection Ownership

Architects must define explicitly when they can approve their own ADRs vs when approval from a higher-level architect or Architecture Review Board (ARB) is required. This suggests technology selection ownership depends on the organization's defined approval criteria and governance model.

# Architect Role Definitions

## Solution Architect
"Solution Architect has mastered fundamental architecture skills and practiced delivery. Responsible for optimizing solution value through delivery and reducing owner risk while ensuring compliance."

## Enterprise Architect
"Enterprise Architect has mastered fundamental skills and practiced within specializations before leading architecture teams. Business technologist who melds business understanding with technology skills to deliver shareholder value."

## Software Architect
"Software Architect has mastered value, use, development and delivery of software-intensive systems. Responsible for value generated from software systems within direct supervision."

## Infrastructure Architect
"Infrastructure Architect provides strategic uses of infrastructure, network, and operations as an asset. Uses mastery of network, computing platform and operations to guide valuable technology investments."

## Information Architect
"Information Architect directs use, integration and storage of information within business units or capabilities. Ensures information is used to organizational advantage while managing storage, retrieval and integration."

## Technology Selection Authority
"IT tool selection for a project must be given by the Global Enterprise architect team, not the business unit IT teams."

## Specialization vs. Generalist Structure
The model employs **four core specializations** (business, information, infrastructure, software) with practitioners advancing to **solution architect** (delivery-focused) or **enterprise architect** (strategic leadership). Enterprise architects must develop competency across all specializations before advancement.

NOTES:
- source: https://martinfowler.com/ieeeSoftware/whoNeedsArchitect.pdf
  what it is: Fowler, "Who Needs an Architect?", IEEE Software 2003 — defines architecture and two architect styles
  relevant passages:
    - "architecture is the decisions that you wish you could get right early in a project, but that you are not necessarily more likely to"
    - "Architecture is about the important stuff. Whatever that is."
    - "Architectus Reloadus is the person who makes all the important decisions. The architect does this because a single mind is needed to ensure a system's conceptual integrity"
    - "the most important activity of Architectus Oryzus is to mentor the development team, to raise their level so that they can take on" (more issues)
    - "an architect's value is inversely proportional to the number of decisions he or she makes"
  takeaway: Fowler does not taxonomize solution/enterprise/technical architects; he frames the architect as owner of "important" (hard-to-reverse) decisions and prefers the mentoring, decision-minimizing style over a central decider.

- source: https://www.enterpriseintegrationpatterns.com/ramblings/79_elevator.html
  what it is: Hohpe's original "Architect Elevator" essay
  relevant passages:
    - "architects ride the elevator up and down to move between the board room and the engine room of a large enterprise."
    - "the worst case scenario happens when people holding relevant information are not allowed to make decisions and the decision makers lack relevant information."
  takeaway: Hohpe defines architects by organizational reach (penthouse to engine room), not by title; decision quality depends on decision rights sitting with those holding information.

- source: https://martinfowler.com/articles/architect-elevator.html
  what it is: Hohpe's expanded Architect Elevator article on martinfowler.com
  relevant passages:
    - "a central architecture team consists of 'high-level' architects positioned close to the penthouse but disconnected from technology innovation"
    - "it makes sense to empower development teams to make architecture decisions, within agreed-upon bounds of general principles or a published IT strategy"
  takeaway: Hohpe's answer to "who owns technology decisions": teams, bounded by principles/IT strategy set at enterprise level — not a central architect.

- source: https://iasa-global.github.io/btabok/job_description.html
  what it is: IASA BTABoK job descriptions for the five architect specializations plus solution/enterprise generalist roles
  relevant passages:
    - "Solution Architect has mastered fundamental architecture skills and practiced delivery. Responsible for optimizing solution value through delivery and reducing owner risk while ensuring compliance."
    - "Enterprise Architect ... Business technologist who melds business understanding with technology skills to deliver shareholder value."
    - "Software Architect ... Responsible for value generated from software systems within direct supervision."
    - "Infrastructure Architect ... Uses mastery of network, computing platform and operations to guide valuable technology investments."
    - "IT tool selection for a project must be given by the Global Enterprise architect team, not the business unit IT teams."
  takeaway: BTABoK: four depth specializations (business, information, infrastructure, software); solution architect = delivery-scoped generalist, enterprise architect = enterprise-strategy generalist; the one explicit tool-selection statement places project tool selection with the enterprise architecture team (statement appears in a job-description example; context unclear).

- source: https://iasa-global.github.io/btabok/architecture_practice.html
  what it is: BTABoK overview of the architecture practice/engagement model
  relevant passages:
    - "It is necessary in this model to deeply align business and solution architects and their deliverables."
  takeaway: No role-level authority over technology selection defined here.

- source: https://www.betterask.erni/the-triple-a-saga-architecture-architects-and-agile-part-ii/
  what it is: ERNI consultancy article distinguishing EA, solution, and software/application architects
  relevant passages:
    - "A Solution Architect will communicate with the Enterprise and Business Architects to understand the constraints to be used for the solution to be created. He may also negotiate with internal teams or external providers about a particular 'service.'"
    - "A Software (or Application or System) Architect will communicate with the Enterprise and/or Solution Architect ... to ensure that the application implementation complies with them."
    - "An Enterprise Architect will be helping the Business Architects understand the Organisation's Application Landscape ... defining processes or quality gates."
  takeaway: Layered constraint flow: EA sets landscape/quality gates -> solution architect applies constraints and sources services -> software architect ensures implementation compliance; stack ownership not stated.

- source: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/aws-certification/latest/solutions-architect-associate-03/solutions-architect-associate-03.html
  what it is: AWS SAA-C03 exam guide
  relevant passages:
    - "intended for individuals who perform a solutions architect role. The exam validates a candidate's ability to design solutions based on the AWS Well-Architected Framework."
    - "Design solutions that incorporate AWS services to meet current business requirements and future projected needs"
    - "Review existing solutions and determine improvements"
  takeaway: AWS's "solutions architect" = designer who chooses among AWS services against business requirements; service selection is intrinsic to the role.

- source: https://aws.amazon.com/certification/certified-solutions-architect-associate/
  what it is: AWS certification marketing page
  relevant passages:
    - "AWS Certified Solutions Architect - Associate is focused on the design of cost and performance optimized solutions."
  takeaway: Same framing, less detail.

- source: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/credentials/certifications/azure-solutions-architect/
  what it is: Microsoft Azure Solutions Architect Expert certification page
  relevant passages:
    - "advising stakeholders and translating business requirements into designs for Azure solutions that align with the Azure Well-Architected Framework and Cloud Adoption Framework for Azure."
    - "you implement solutions on Azure by partnering with various other job roles, including: Developers, Administrators, Security engineers, Data engineers"
    - "You should manage how decisions in each area affect an overall solution."
  takeaway: Microsoft's solutions architect owns the whole-solution design and cross-area decision trade-offs; partners with (does not supervise) developers.

- source: https://cloud.google.com/learn/certification/cloud-architect
  what it is: Google Professional Cloud Architect certification page
  relevant passages:
    - "leverage Google Cloud technologies to design, develop, and manage robust, secure, scalable, efficient, cost-effective, highly available, and flexible solutions that drive business objectives."
    - "proficient in enterprise cloud strategy, solution design, workload migration approaches, deployment and orchestration, optimization, and architectural best practices."
  takeaway: Google uses "Cloud Architect" (not "solutions architect"); scope spans enterprise cloud strategy through solution design and infrastructure.

- source: https://martinfowler.com/articles/scaling-architecture-conversationally.html
  what it is: Andrew Harmel-Law's Architecture Advice Process article
  relevant passages:
    - "Anyone can make an architectural decision" but must "consult two groups: The first is everyone who will be meaningfully affected by the decision. The second is people with expertise in the area."
    - "ADRs serve to reinforce the Advice Process by making it a requirement on ADR authors to capture and record all advice they get."
    - "Decisions taken to the AAF are still owned and made by the originators. The only thing other attendees can do is offer advice."
    - "Your own Technology Radar" captures "your local version of the technology trends you see across your organisation"
  takeaway: Decision ownership sits with the originator (anyone); ADRs record advice; the Architecture Advisory Forum replaces an approving ARB; an internal tech radar is a team-maintained guardrail.

- source: https://www.thoughtworks.com/radar/techniques/lightweight-architecture-decision-records
  what it is: Thoughtworks Radar entry, Adopt
  relevant passages:
    - "a technique for capturing important architectural decisions along with their context and consequences."
    - "We recommend storing these details in source control, instead of a wiki or website"
  takeaway: ADRs are Adopt (2018); authored by team members, kept with code; no single owning role named.

- source: https://www.thoughtworks.com/en-us/radar/techniques/architecture-advice-process
  what it is: Thoughtworks Radar entry, Trial (Apr 2025)
  relevant passages:
    - "Anyone can make any architectural decision, provided they seek advice from those affected and those with relevant expertise."
    - "The traditional approach of Architecture Review Boards is counterproductive, often hindering workflow and correlating with low organizational performance."
  takeaway: Thoughtworks (citing State of DevOps) positions ARBs as an anti-pattern and the advice process as the replacement.

- source: https://theartofcto.com/frameworks/architecture-review-process
  what it is: Practitioner framework for an ARB-based review process with RACI and scorecard
  relevant passages:
    - "Responsible: Engineer | Accountable: Engineer | Consulted: ARB"
    - "4.0+: Approve | 3.0-3.9: Approve with conditions | under 3.0: Reject or redesign"
  takeaway: Even an ARB-centric model makes the proposing engineer accountable, with the ARB consulted/scoring; ADR self-approval thresholds not defined.

CONFLICTS/GAPS:
- Ownership of technology selection splits three ways: BTABoK's job-description text places project tool selection with the enterprise architecture team; Hohpe and Harmel-Law/Thoughtworks place it with delivery teams bounded by principles/strategy; theartofcto RACI makes the engineer accountable with ARB consulted. No source assigns stack/platform selection to the "solutions architect" title by name — vendors imply it (AWS "design solutions that incorporate AWS services") but only within their own platform.
- "Technical architect" is not defined by any opened source; ERNI conflates software/application/system architect; BTABoK's nearest analogue is infrastructure architect.
- Fowler gives no role taxonomy at all; his contribution is the decision-centric definition of architecture and the value-inversely-proportional-to-decisions rule.
- Gartner/major-consultancy taxonomy not opened (ERNI is a mid-size consultancy); IASA remains the only formal body-of-knowledge taxonomy opened.
- Technology radar ownership: Harmel-Law describes it as organization-local and maintained collaboratively; no source names an owning role.
